blocks.x: “Being easy to please is often mistaken for having no needs at all.” ~Unknown
We’d been together four years when my husband turned to me in the car and asked, completely out of nowhere, “What’s your favorite color?”
I laughed, assuming he was joking. He wasn’t.
“I’m serious,” he said. “I realized I don’t actually know. I know mine’s blue. I don’t know yours.”

I opened my mouth to answer, and nothing came out. Not because I didn’t have a favorite color. Because I genuinely couldn’t remember the last time anyone had asked me a question like that, and my mind went blank trying to locate an answer that belonged only to me.
“I don’t know,” I finally said. “I’ve never really thought about it.”
He looked at me like I’d told him I didn’t know my own middle name.
For most of my adult life, “easy” was the highest compliment I thought I could earn.

Easy to date. Easy to room with. Easy to work with. My college roommate used to tell people, “She’s so chill, she genuinely doesn’t care what we do,” and I wore that sentence like an award. My first serious boyfriend told his mother I was “low-maintenance,” and I remember feeling a warm flush of pride, like I’d passed some invisible test.
I didn’t examine it beyond that. Being easy meant being good. Being easy meant people wanted me around.

What I didn’t examine—what took me years to even notice—was that being “easy” required a constant, invisible sanding-down of my own preferences. Where do you want to eat? Anywhere is fine. What movie do you want to watch? Whatever you’re in the mood for. Where should we go on vacation? I don’t mind. You pick.
I said some version of those sentences so many times that I stopped noticing I was saying them. They weren’t even really answers. They were reflexes.
The car ride with my husband cracked something open that I spent the next several months poking at, uncomfortably, like a bruise I kept forgetting was there.

I started paying attention to how often I did this. Not just with him—with everyone. A friend would ask where I wanted to grab coffee, and I’d feel a tiny jolt of panic before saying, “Oh, wherever’s easiest for you.” My sister would ask what I wanted for my birthday, and I’d say, “Honestly, don’t worry about it. I don’t need anything.” And I’d mean it in the sense that I had genuinely stopped letting myself want things enough to name them.
I brought it up with my husband a few weeks later, half-joking, half-not. “I think I actually don’t know what I like anymore.”
He didn’t laugh. He said, “I’ve kind of noticed that. I used to think you were just really chill. Now I think you might just be really good at disappearing.”
That sentence sat in my chest for days.

I want to be clear that nobody forced this on me. My husband never once said he needed me to be easy. My friends never demanded I have no preferences. If anything, the people closest to me kept gently asking what I wanted, over and over, the way you’d tap on a door to see if anyone’s home.
I was the one who kept answering “whatever’s fine” long after it stopped being true.

I think I learned somewhere, a long time before any of these relationships, that having strong preferences made me a target. Growing up, my parents’ moods could shift a room in seconds, and I got very good, very young, at reading which way the wind was blowing and adjusting myself to match it before anyone had to ask. Agreeing was safer than wanting. Wanting gave people something to say no to.
By the time I was an adult, “I don’t care, whatever you want” wasn’t a personality trait. It was a decades-old survival reflex wearing a very convincing disguise.
The hardest part wasn’t realizing this. The hardest part was trying to undo it.
A few weeks after the color conversation, my husband asked where I wanted to go for dinner, and I made myself say an actual restaurant. Not “wherever,” not “you pick,” but an actual name, out loud.
He blinked. “Oh! Yeah, let’s do that.”
That was it. No argument. No disappointment. No one accused me of being difficult. And still, my heart was pounding like I’d done something reckless.
I sat in the passenger seat on the way there, feeling this strange mix of pride and exposure, like I’d walked outside without a coat I’d worn so long I forgot it was optional.

It kept happening like that, in small, almost embarrassingly tiny ways. Telling a friend I actually wanted to see a different movie than the one she suggested. Saying I didn’t want to host Thanksgiving that year. Admitting, out loud, that I do have a favorite color, and it’s green, and I like it because it reminds me of the woods behind my childhood house, a detail nobody had ever bothered to ask me about because I’d never once given them the opening.
Every single time, I braced for the relationship to reveal itself as conditional. For someone to say, “Actually, I liked you better when you didn’t want things.” No one ever did.

I’ve since wondered how many of my relationships were built on a version of me that wasn’t quite real. Not fake, exactly. Just edited. A person-shaped space where my actual preferences used to be, filled in instead with whatever would keep things smooth.
I don’t think anyone loved that edited version more than they would have loved the real one. I think I just never gave them the chance to find out.

My husband and I still laugh about the color conversation sometimes, though it doesn’t feel entirely like a joke to me even now. It was the first crack in a wall I didn’t know I’d built. Four years into a marriage, and he was asking a question you’d expect on a first date, because I had made myself so easy that I’d made myself unknown.

I’m not easy anymore, not in the way I used to be. I have opinions about restaurants. I have a favorite color. I’ve disappointed people in small, survivable ways, and the relationships held anyway, which was the thing I never quite believed until I tested it myself, over and over, in tiny increments.

If I’m honest, I still catch the old reflex sometimes. Someone asks what I want, and “whatever’s fine” rises up automatically, halfway out of my mouth before I stop it. But I stop it more often now. I make myself answer the real question underneath: not what’s easiest to say, but “What do I actually want?”
It still feels a little dangerous every time. Wanting things out loud always does, if you spent long enough believing it wasn’t safe.
But nobody’s left yet. And every time they stay, it gets a little easier to believe they were never staying for the easy version in the first place.
They were staying for me.
